newsitem.title: FRANCE: In French election, all sides act as opposition.
newsitem.headline: In French election, all sides act as opposition.

text.p: In France's snap parliamentary election, even conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe seems to be campaigning on an opposition ticket.

The ruling centre-right coalition and the main opposition Socialists both have good reasons to blame the other for problems of record unemployment, spluttering growth, social inequalities and creeping political sleaze.
Both have done so in the first week of campaigning for the May 25-June 1 election, bringing mutual charges of amnesia as well as confusion among voters.

More than a fifth of voters do not state a choice when asked by pollsters who they will vote for, many others who do say they may still change their minds. Surveys so far show the centre-right is likely to retain a slimmer majority.

"Our candidates will be the candidates of change," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said in an interview with the Journal du Dimanche on Sunday, accusing the centre-right of wrecking a caring society since it won a landslide in the 1993 parliamentary election.
"The French people will surprise" in the election, he predicted, despite polls showing the centre-right is likely to retain a reduced majority.

Juppe kicked off his campaign last week by squarely blaming the Socialists, with a call to supporters: "Let's take the offensive against those who are responsible for the terrible failure of the 80s and 90s."

He said 14 years under late Socialist President Mitterrand, succeeded by conservative Jacques Chirac in 1995, had "robbed society of its traditional points of reference" and had sapped France economically, socially, morally and politically.

"We have created the bases for a recovery of our country after years of decline," Juppe said, saying his painful austerity cure would pave the way to an economic revival and a single European currency from 1999.
Jospin blasted Juppe's "diatribes against the Socialists who have been in opposition for four years."

He accused President Jacques Chirac of dissolving parliament almost 10 months early in hopes of securing re-election for his allies to pave the way to a new bout of painful austerity to qualify for a single currency, the euro.
The government has denied that a new round of fiscal austerity beyond that already planned is needed.

France's electoral system, under which the president's seven-year term does not run in tandem with the five years of the National Assembly, is providing an alibi for all sides to adopt the mantle of the opposition.

The centre-right won 80 percent of the seats in the National Assembly at the last election in 1993 when voters dumped the Socialists, blamed for high unemployment and increasing corruption in politics.

That forced Mitterrand to spend the final two years of his rule in an uneasy "cohabitation" with Juppe's centre-right predecessor, prime minister Edouard Balladur. The president has responsibility for foreign affairs and defence.

Apart from campaigning against the Socialists' record and presenting his policies as a needed cure, Juppe has targeted Jospin as a hostage to the smaller Communist party, with whom Jospin would probably have to cooperate in case of victory.

Jospin favours a single currency on certain conditions, Communist leader Robert Hue is bitterly against. "I can see Mr Juppe is trying to scare people, but with who or with what?" Jospin said. "Maybe he hasn't noticed the Soviet Union no longer exists."
In an editorial for the Journal du Dimanche, commentator Alain Genestar said the campaign had failed to live up to expectations with France facing a crossroads in Europe.

He said the three big questions debated so far were: If the right wins, will Juppe remain prime minister? If the left wins, will there be Communist ministers? How many candidates should take part in a televised debate?
"Difficult to be more simplistic," he commented.
